item.title: If we stop, we lose
item.content:encoded:
It's been a rather morale draining era in the making websites industry since the wider tech industry decided to gamble everything on LLMs. We at Piccalilli see it amongst the community and feel it ourselves.

You'll also have noticed the velocity of posts has slowed down somewhat on this website with no new courses announced either. There's a couple of reasons for that. First, the numbers have taken a dramatic tumble — industry-wide — but also, aside from being very busy in the studio, we've been tired. Swimming against this particular current will do that, even for folks like us that have always operated like that.

Something else you might have noticed is that a lot of other educators have gone a lot quieter this year too. I'm writing this post today to hopefully try and fix that.

A shot in the arm

I had a delightful conversation with CSS-Tricks head honcho, Geoff, yesterday. Aside from the excellent vibes as a result of CSS-Tricks being back as an independent publisher, I started in a rather glum mood. After spending a few minutes listening to Geoff's exciting plans though I really perked up.

We're nowhere near CSS-Tricks here, but we've always looked up to them as an example of what years and years at the top of your game looks like. Sure, the DigitalOcean acquisition didn't work out, but the fact that the publication is not only back, but well up for the fight against the supposed death of web education is really inspiring to me. I needed that win, as did many others.

I needed it so much, it's spurred me on to write this article to hopefully give us all a shot in the arm.

There is no inevitable future and education will always matter

A comment I see all the time is "we don't need articles and courses because we can just ask an LLM now", which I guess is true, but I could also eat an entire can of spray cheese. It ain't gonna nourish me!

AI technologies have given anyone the ability to bring their ideas to life, but to produce a high quality end product that actually works for the people it needs to work for requires experience, specialist skills and creativity. That is a reality, which aside from Silicon Valley's best efforts, is why there are still working developers out there, regardless of "frontier model" power. Human developer's experience is necessary because LLM outputs still (somehow, after hundreds of billions of investment) fall short.

Let me repeat that: their experience is necessary. Who inevitably contributed to that experience? Yep: educators.

Let's get to work then

This article is mainly addressed to fellow educators, but also to people that write on their personal blogs. You must keep going because people still need us. If we don't, we lose.

The LLM era is opening up an enormous skills gap that's only going to get wider as the industry continues to pull up the ladder, eliminating entry level positions. We're needed to help people really understand how all of this stuff works, so even if they are at the behest of LLM mandates, they can produce better outputs.

The technology is going nowhere — that toothpaste is long out of the tube — but how many other hype cycles have underwhelmed in the end?

Spoiler, all of them

The economics of the AI industry simply do not work and the technology — albeit ever-present in development — will fall into its actual place eventually, as a niche tool.

With all of this in mind, we're fighting back too, so I'm opening up the guest authoring on this site again, just like Geoff is over on CSS-Tricks. I'm determined to get this website cooking again and I would love to share your words with the rest of the industry.

Let's buck up our ideas and get cracking, everyone. There's lots to teach and I know we've got plenty of fight left in us.

To quote our very own Mat Marquis:

You and me, we’re not done until we say we’re done

Don't let the bastards grind you down.

item.title: Native masonry layouts with CSS grid lanes
item.content:encoded:
Native masonry layouts have been a long time coming to CSS and after years of debate over how they should work and fit into the language, we finally have display: grid-lanes.

If you want the full backstory on how we got here, Sunkanmi Fafowora has a great overview of the grid-lanes announcement over on CSS-Tricks. Here, I want to focus on the technical side of masonry, why it took so long to get right, and how display: grid-lanes works.

How we got here

Masonry has been a long-running CSS challenge. Back in 2017, Rachel Andrew opened a CSSWG issue about creating a native Pinterest-style layout. As Rachel noted back then, the closest native CSS got to this was multi-column layout (column-count), but that flows items top-to-bottom. Masonry needs to flow items across rows, tightly packing them into whatever column currently has the most available vertical space.

That same year, Tab Atkins-Bittner shared a clever Grid hack to approximate the layout. It relied on knowing each item’s height in advance, making it less practical for dynamic content.

.hacky-masonry {
        display: grid;
        grid: auto-flow dense 1px / repeat(3, 1fr);
        }
        
        /* Manually set each item's row span */
        .item {
        grid-row: span 50; /* Matches the item's 50px height */
        }

As cool as this hack was, having to know the exact height of every item ahead of time wasn’t very practical, especially when you’re dealing with dynamic content, where heights can change. When I spoke with Tab Atkins-Bittner for my piece on the evolution of CSS Masonry, they put the broader challenge of designing CSS layouts this way:

“Flexbox was the first of the modern layout algorithms; we made a lot of mistakes and missteps while writing it, because we were trying to figure out how a modern layout model should work.”

That same process of figuring things out played a role in masonry's development and until CSS had a better answer, many of us ended up reaching for David DeSandro’s legendary Masonry.js library instead.

But the challenge wasn't just figuring out how to make masonry work in CSS. There was also the question of how it should fit into the language. Should it be part of Flexbox, an extension of Grid, or its own display value? For years, the CSS Working Group went back and forth without settling on a final syntax.

Mozilla first explored adding masonry to Grid, and WebKit later picked up that approach. It lets you keep display: grid and use a special value for the tracks to enable masonry.

.masonry {
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
        grid-template-rows: masonry;
        }

This kept Grid's familiar column definitions while letting the browser pack items vertically instead of aligning them into rows. You can read more about WebKit's reasoning in Help us choose the final syntax for Masonry in CSS.

Google's Chromium team had a different take. They argued that masonry's layout algorithm was different enough from Grid to deserve its own layout mode, proposed as display: masonry .

.masonry {
        display: masonry;
        masonry-template-tracks: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
        gap: 1rem;
        }

Their reasoning, along with an alternative syntax, is explained in An alternative proposal for CSS masonry.

The debate continued through several rounds of proposals, including WebKit's broader item-flow idea for unifying aspects of Grid and Flexbox, but that approach was eventually dropped in favor of a simpler direction.

In January 2025, the CSS Working Group agreed to reuse CSS Grid's track-definition and placement properties for masonry. By December 2025, the group had settled on a name for the new layout mode, grid-lanes. WebKit announced the direction in Introducing CSS Grid Lanes.

How grid lanes works

The nice thing about display: grid-lanes is that you don't have to figure out where every item goes yourself. You define the tracks along one axis, just as you would with regular CSS Grid and the browser handles placement along the other.

For a typical masonry layout, that means defining your columns with grid-template-columns and letting the browser stack items into whichever lane makes the most sense.

You still get familiar Grid properties like grid-template-columns, repeat(), minmax(), gap, and explicit placement. Under the hood, though, Grid Lanes uses a different layout algorithm: it maintains tracks along the grid axis and packs items along the stacking axis. That makes it possible to build responsive masonry layouts without calculating item heights yourself.

A Basic Masonry Layout

.masonry {
        display: grid-lanes;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr));
        gap: 1rem;
        }

This defines as many columns as fit, with each column at least 14rem wide. The browser handles the rest, placing items into lanes as it lays them out. Unlike regular Grid, items don't need to share row heights, so each lane can grow independently.

Here’s how this layout would look:

The fill algorithm

Unlike regular CSS Grid, Grid Lanes doesn't try to line everything up in rows. Instead, the browser keeps track of how much space each lane takes up and uses that to decide where the next item should go.

The process is pretty simple:

  1. Check how much each lane is filled.
  2. Place the next item in a suitable lane, usually the shortest one.
  3. Update that lane's position and repeat.

For example, with three columns, the first three cards go into separate lanes. If column 2 is now the shortest, the next card goes there.

.masonry {
        display: grid-lanes;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
        gap: 1rem;
        }

Controlling item placement

Most of the time, you'll let the browser handle placement. But you can still use familiar Grid properties when you want more control. For example, grid-column: span 2 lets an item span two columns instead of occupying just one.

.featured-item {
        grid-column: span 2;
        }

The browser actually places these explicitly positioned and spanning items first, before it runs the masonry algorithm for the rest of the auto-placed items. Spanning items affects how the remaining space is distributed, so placement can get more complicated than simply choosing the shortest lane, especially in larger layouts with lots of moving pieces.

Since items can appear in a different visual order from their source order, it's also worth checking that the layout still makes sense when read from the HTML. This matters for accessibility, too, as screen readers generally follow the document order rather than the visual layout. We’ll cover this in more detail later.

A note on fit-tolerance

The Grid Lanes spec is still evolving, but its direction is becoming clearer. The CSS Working Group dropped the broader item-* proposal for unifying flow controls across layout modes and settled on display: grid-lanes for masonry. Another change is the rename of flow-tolerance to fit-tolerance, a property that helps control how the browser chooses between lanes of similar heights.

Say you have two lanes; one is 400px tall and the other is 398px. The second lane is technically shorter, but only by 2px. With a tolerance of 1em , the browser can treat both lanes as close enough in height and choose the lane that better preserves the source order, rather than always picking the shortest one. This can help prevent items from jumping ahead of earlier items just to fill tiny gaps.

Here’s how different values affect the layout:

.masonry {
        fit-tolerance: 0; /* favor the shortest lane */
        }
        
        .masonry {
        fit-tolerance: 1em; /* Treat lanes within 1em as close enough */
        }
        
        .masonry {
        fit-tolerance: infinite; /* Prioritize source order over compact packing */
        }

A value of 0 favors tighter packing, while a larger tolerance gives the browser more flexibility to keep items closer to their source order. infinite prioritizes source order, even if that leaves more empty space in the layout. The default is normal, which resolves to 1em.

FYI

infinite prioritizes source order, but it won’t guarantee it in every case. Similarly, 0 removes the tolerance for treating lanes of similar heights as equivalent.

Switching directions

Masonry doesn't have to flow vertically. With Grid Lanes, the tracks you define also determine the direction items are packed in. When you define grid-template-columns, items are packed vertically into columns. When you define grid-template-rows, items are packed horizontally into rows. The first is the familiar Pinterest-style layout, while the second creates a brick-like arrangement.

Check out this Waterfall and Brick demo, by ICS Creative, to switch between the two layouts and see the difference. Both use display: grid-lanes, just with different track definitions.

The WebKit team has also published the Field Guide to Grid Lanes. It includes an interactive playground, a reference for the different properties and values, and six demos covering layouts like photo galleries, recipe cards, timelines, and pinboards.

Subgrids in masonry layouts

One of the arguments for keeping masonry part of CSS Grid was that it would preserve features like subgrid.

If masonry had its own display: masonry layout mode, getting nested elements to align with their parent's grid tracks could have required changes across multiple CSS specifications. Keeping masonry within the Grid model means subgrid can work alongside it.

Say you're building a masonry layout of recipe cards, each with a title, an image, and a list of ingredients. subgrid lets the cards use their parent's grid tracks rather than defining their own, making it easier to align their internal elements.

.masonry-container {
        display: grid-lanes;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(300px, 1fr));
        }
        
        .recipe-card {
        display: grid;
        /* The card's internal columns align with the parent masonry grid */
        grid-template-columns: subgrid;
        }

Where we’re at today

Grid Lanes has come a long way from the early proposals and workarounds, but there's still work to do. The specification is an Editor’s Draft, which means details can change as the CSS Working Group continues to refine the layout model.

Browser support is another thing to keep an eye on. As of writing this article, Grid Lanes works in Safari 26.4 and later, but support in other browsers is still evolving. Check Can I Use for the latest updates, and consider using a simpler fallback for browsers that don't support it.

Wrapping up

Grid Lanes has come a long way from the early proposals and workarounds. Here's a quick recap of where things stand now:

  • Masonry uses display: grid-lanes as a separate layout mode.
  • Lanes are defined by grid-template-columns or grid-template-rows.
  • Items are automatically placed into lanes based on available space.
  • fit-tolerance controls how much difference between lanes is treated as a tie.
  • The DOM source order stays intact, even when the visual order differs.
  • Unsupported browsers can use a simpler fallback layout.
